title: Polynomial-time recognition of the 3-sphere
formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm deciding whether a finite simplicial triangulation of a closed connected piecewise-linear \(3\)-manifold is piecewise-linearly homeomorphic to the standard \(3\)-sphere?

Precisely, let \(\mathcal P\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) be the promised encodings below, and let \(S(x)\) assert that the encoded complex is PL-homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^{4}\). Does there exist one uniform deterministic Turing machine \(M\), an integer \(C\ge1\), and an integer \(d\ge0\) such that
\[
\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ \exists b\in\{0,1\}\
\left[
H_{M}\bigl(x,C(|x|+1)^{d},b\bigr)
\ \land\
\bigl(x\in\mathcal P\ \Rightarrow\ (b=1\Longleftrightarrow S(x))\bigr)
\right]?
\]
Here \(H_{M}(x,t,b)\) means that \(M\) halts within \(t\) transitions with output bit \(b\). The running-time bound holds on every binary string, including malformed encodings and inputs outside the manifold promise; correctness is required on \(\mathcal P\). The machine and both polynomial constants are fixed before the input is chosen.
definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex on \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is a collection \(K\) of subsets of \([m]\), closed under taking subsets and containing every singleton. Its elements are simplices; a simplex with \(r+1\) vertices has dimension \(r\). A tetrahedron is a simplex with four vertices.

An input complex is given by integers \(m\ge4\) and \(N\ge1\), and \(N\) distinct tetrahedra
\(\tau_{j}=\{v_{j1},v_{j2},v_{j3},v_{j4}\}\), where
\[
1\le v_{j1}<v_{j2}<v_{j3}<v_{j4}\le m.
\]
The quadruples are listed in strictly increasing lexicographic order, and every vertex in \([m]\) occurs. Define
\[
K_{x}=\{\sigma\subseteq[m]:\ \sigma\subseteq\tau_{j}
\text{ for some }j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\}.
\]
All lower-dimensional faces are implicit. Thus the listed tetrahedra are exactly the maximal simplices. There are no coordinates, edge lengths or geometric drawings in the input.

Fix a binary encoding as follows. For a nonnegative integer \(r\), let \(b(r)\) be the ordinary binary representation of \(r+1\), with no leading zero, and let \(\ell=|b(r)|\). Encode \(r\) by \(1^{\ell}0b(r)\). The input string is the concatenation of the codes of \(m,N\), followed by the codes of \(v_{11},v_{12},v_{13},v_{14},v_{21},\ldots,v_{N4}\) in that order, with no trailing bits. A syntactically valid string parses uniquely and obeys the preceding inequalities, ordering and vertex-coverage conditions. Set \(L=|x|\), the total number of input bits. Since every vertex occurs, \(m\le4N\); these explicit encodings have length \(O(N\log(N+2))\).

The geometric realization is the polyhedron
\[
|K|=\left\{(a_{1},\ldots,a_{m})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m}:
\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}=1,\ 
\{i:a_{i}>0\}\in K\right\}.
\]
Each abstract simplex is realized as the convex hull of its coordinate unit vectors. A finite geometric simplicial complex is a finite collection of convex hulls of affinely independent finite point sets, containing all their faces, with the intersection of any two simplices empty or a common face. A subdivision of a realization \(|K|\) is such a geometric complex with underlying set \(|K|\), each of whose simplices is contained in an original simplex, and for which every original simplex is the union of simplices of the subdivision. New vertices may be arbitrary real points; they are not additional input data.

Two finite complexes are PL-homeomorphic if they have finite subdivisions whose abstract simplicial complexes are isomorphic. An isomorphism is a bijection of their vertices carrying simplices to simplices in both directions; its affine extension on each simplex supplies the piecewise-linear homeomorphism. There is no required bound on the size of these subdivisions in the definition of the topological property. For \(r\ge1\), \(\Delta^{r}\) is the full simplex on \(r+1\) vertices and \(\partial\Delta^{r}\) consists of all its proper faces. The standard PL \(3\)-sphere is \(|\partial\Delta^{4}|\); the standard PL \(2\)-sphere is \(|\partial\Delta^{3}|\).

For a vertex \(v\) define its link by
\[
\operatorname{lk}_{K}(v)=
\{\sigma\in K:v\notin\sigma,\ \sigma\cup\{v\}\in K\}.
\]
A link has as its vertex set the union of its simplices; when realizing it, use those vertices as the coordinate indices. The same definitions apply to any finite vertex set by replacing \([m]\) with that set. The promise set \(\mathcal P\) consists of syntactically valid strings such that the graph with vertex set \([m]\) and edges the two-element simplices of \(K_{x}\) is connected, and every vertex link is PL-homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^{3}\). This is the simplicial formulation of a closed connected PL \(3\)-manifold: finite realization gives compactness, and the spherical-link condition gives the local manifold condition without boundary. No orientation, homology calculation, fundamental-group presentation or certificate of the promise is supplied. Nonorientable manifolds are permitted by the promise. For every binary string \(x\), define \(S(x)\) to be false if \(x\) is not syntactically valid, and otherwise to mean that \(K_{x}\) is PL-homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^{4}\).

The machine model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with finite control, one read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes. Its tape alphabet is \(\{0,1,\#,\square\}\), with \(\square\) blank. Tape cells have nonnegative integer indices and every head initially scans cell zero. The input tape initially holds exactly \(x\) followed by blanks. One transition reads the symbols under the heads, changes the state, writes at most one symbol on each work tape and moves each head by at most one cell; a left move at cell zero stays there. The two halting states output zero and one, respectively. Each transition costs one unit, so all parsing and arithmetic are charged at the bit level. The number of tapes, state set and transition table are independent of \(L\). There is no advice, randomness, oracle or unit-cost operation on unbounded integers.

An answer of one is required for every promised triangulation of the standard PL sphere, and an answer of zero for every other promised manifold. For all other binary strings either bit is permitted, but the same uniform polynomial time bound is mandatory. Neither efficient performance on sampled inputs nor an algorithm restricted to a proper subclass of the promised manifolds meets this definition.

context_blocks.text: Schleimer proves that 3-sphere recognition lies in NP: sphere instances have certificates of polynomial length that can be verified in polynomial time. The same source records earlier decision algorithms. These are different guarantees from finding the correct answer deterministically in polynomial time.

The source allows tetrahedra glued by face pairings and deliberately leaves the precise binary format unspecified. This card retains its existing finite simplicial-complex representation and closed connected PL-manifold promise, and now fixes a concrete explicit encoding and bit-cost machine model. Its local-link formulation states that promise precisely.

Zentner proves a conditional negative-certificate result under the generalized Riemann hypothesis. His Theorem 11.2 is stated for integer homology spheres represented by Heegaard diagrams; the 2026 problem list records the resulting coNP status for sphere recognition with the same hypothesis. Such a certificate statement does not imply membership in P.
Lackenby's unconditional theorem concerns certifying that a knot is nontrivial. It must not be substituted for an unconditional coNP theorem for 3-sphere recognition.

The 2026 K3 problem list asks explicitly whether 3-sphere recognition has a polynomial-time algorithm. It also records that such an algorithm would make unknot recognition polynomial-time when the knot is supplied by a diagram.

why: Recognizing the simplest closed three-dimensional manifold is a basic test of whether global topological structure can be determined efficiently from local combinatorial data. A polynomial-time algorithm would also give polynomial-time unknot recognition for diagram input, while separating decidability and short certificates from efficient decision in a central example of computational topology.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed existence proposition, including one machine, its uniform polynomial clock on all binary strings and both correctness directions on \(\mathcal P\), or a complete Lean proof of its full logical negation.

Explicitly, the negative answer must prove
\[
\forall M\ \forall C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall d\in\mathbb N_{0}\
\exists x\in\{0,1\}^{*}
\]
such that, writing \(t=C(|x|+1)^{d}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\bigl(\neg H_{M}(x,t,0)\land\neg H_{M}(x,t,1)\bigr)\\
&\quad\lor\
\left[
x\in\mathcal P\ \land\
\left(
\bigl(H_{M}(x,t,1)\land\neg S(x)\bigr)
\lor
\bigl(H_{M}(x,t,0)\land S(x)\bigr)
\right)
\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus every candidate machine and polynomial clock must fail either the total time bound or correctness on a promised input. The witness input may depend on the candidate and clock. A lower bound for one algorithm, a conditional complexity implication, NP or coNP membership, or a proof of decidability alone does not decide this unconditional target.

sentences: The input is an explicit finite simplicial complex promised to triangulate a closed connected PL three-manifold.
The question asks whether one deterministic algorithm can recognize the standard three-sphere in time polynomial in the total input bit length.
The polynomial bound must hold on all binary inputs, while correct answers are required on the promised manifold inputs.
Sphere recognition is decidable and has polynomially verifiable positive certificates, with the checked negative-certificate result depending on the generalized Riemann hypothesis.
The 2026 K3 problem list retains the polynomial-time question, whose resolution would also affect the complexity of unknot recognition.

checked_sources: Read data/cards/TCS-7292.json and docs/RULES.md. The existing card already fixes deterministic Turing computation, finite simplicial complexes represented by maximal tetrahedra, a closed connected PL 3-manifold promise, and a polynomial time bound on every encoding. The revision retains all of these choices. Importance 91 and category are assessed and must be preserved unchanged.

Read the actual 2011 publisher offprint of Schleimer, not only its arXiv landing page: Section 3 pp. 186–188 defines binary instance size and Turing-machine computation, allows face-pairing triangulations more general than simplicial complexes, and notes the O(n log n) explicit encoding scale. Theorem 3.4 gives polynomial-time manifold recognition, and Theorem 3.5 gives polynomial-time homology-sphere recognition. Theorem 15.1 pp. 211–212 proves NP membership. The arXiv v1 submission is dated 5 July 2004 and calls its main result Theorem 16.1; the retrieved v1 PDF carries an automatically typeset 26 October 2018 date that must not be misrepresented as a new submission.

The exact tetrahedron-list binary serialization is an editorial convention completing the existing representation. The card does not silently switch to face identifications, add an orientability or homology-sphere promise, or require the input to carry witnesses of the manifold promise. The subdivision-based definition allows arbitrary finite geometric subdivisions, without an invented polynomial size bound. Read the local-link and low-dimensional PL statements in Friedl–Nagel–Orson–Powell, Theorem 3.6 p. 18 and Proposition 3.11 pp. 20–21. These support the explicit closed PL manifold interpretation.

Checked Zentner arXiv metadata through v4, submitted 2 February 2018, and read Section 11 pp. 67–68 of that PDF. Theorem 11.2 is explicitly for integer homology 3-spheres given by Heegaard diagrams and assumes GRH. It is not literally a theorem stated for this card's exact simplicial bit encoding; the later K3 source records the standard triangulated sphere-recognition consequence with the same assumption. Neither a homology-sphere promise nor GRH has been inserted into the card's target.

Read K3 preliminary author PDF Section 3.2 pp. 150–151: Problem 3.27(b) asks for polynomial-time 3-sphere recognition, Remark (5) retains GRH for coNP, and Remark (7) records the polynomial implication to unknot recognition when given a knot diagram. The book is AMS Mathematical Surveys and Monographs 295, 2026; checked editors' institutional pages for that publication metadata. Only the saved preliminary PDF's pagination and statements are claimed checked. Its exact within-2026 revision date is not specified.

Audited a conflicting assertion in Joswig–Lofano–Lutz–Tsuruga, Frontiers of sphere recognition in practice, Journal of Applied and Computational Topology 6 (2022), DOI 10.1007/s41468-022-00092-8. Its introduction attributes unconditional sphere coNP to Lackenby (2021), but its bibliography points to The efficient certification of knottedness and Thurston norm. Downloaded the cited paper's arXiv v3, 12 April 2021, and read Theorem 1.1 p. 1 and nearby main statements: the unconditional result is knottedness in NP. Its irreducibility result has a positive first-Betti-number restriction. The checked citation does not substantiate unconditional coNP for all 3-sphere recognition; the 2026 K3 list independently retains the GRH caveat. The draft does not propagate the conflicting claim.

Bounded later searches through 16 September 2026 included 3-sphere recognition with polynomial time, coNP, unconditional, 2025/2026, and a post-April-2026 date range. Checked the 2024 Recognition of Seifert fibered spaces with boundary is in NP introduction, which also retains GRH for sphere coNP. Read the opening of Carmesin–Lichev arXiv:2003.00442v1, 1 March 2020, later DCG 67 (2022), pp. 1097–1123: its constructions concern a particular embeddability approach and do not settle polynomial sphere recognition. No checked later source supplies the requested deterministic polynomial-time algorithm or a full lower bound against all such algorithms. This is a bounded source/status audit, not exhaustive proof verification.

The full negative criterion includes failure of the time bound even on an unpromised string, exactly matching the retained positive all-string clock. Among machines satisfying a uniform polynomial clock on all strings, failure must instead occur on a promised input. The expanded formula also includes nontermination. Constant C and degree d are chosen once per candidate program, not per triangulation.
